title: Native megafauna (Bison bison) act as a surprising inhibitor of cedar tree expansion in a Great Plains grassland

plot_number: 8 per site, clustered in pairs (4 sites within sites, 2 exclosures at each)
herbivore_manipulation_notes: Introduced 2021

citation: Tanentzap et al 2023 Biological Conservation
title: Trade-offs between passive and trophic rewilding for biodiversity and ecosystem functioning
study_notes: Knepp wildland, proper trophic rewilding experiment, variety of large herbivores introduced from 2009 onwards, exclosures established before that
land_use_history_notes: former arable farmland, never exposed to heavy grazing
management_notes: basically nothing, except some removals to keep herd structure
introduced_herbivores: Bos primigenius taurus; Equus ferus caballus; Sus scrofa, Cervus elaphus, Dama dama
herbivore_manipulation_notes: In 2009, the entire site was stock-fenced and Old English longhorn cattle (Bos primigenius primigenius), Exmoor ponies (E. ferus caballus), and Tamworth pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) were introduced. These are all older domesticated breeds intended to act as functional analogues for extinct auroch (B. primigenius taurus), tarpan (E. ferus ferus), and wild boar (Sus scrofa scrofa), respectively (Bunzel-Drüke, 2001; Tree, 2018). Non-native fallow deer (Dama dama) and native red deer (Cervus elaphus) were also introduced respectively in 2009 and 2013. The animals roam freely alongside native roe (Capreolus capreolus) deer, as their home ranges in open habitats of southern England are typically smaller than that of our study site
density_high_megafauna: 0.27 Bos primigenius taurus; 0.03 Equus ferus caballus; 0.04 Sus scrofa, 0.02 Cervus elaphus, 0.26 Dama dama

citation: Plassmann et al 2010 Applied Vegetation Science
title: Effects of long-term grazing management on sand dune vegetation of high conservation interest
study_notes: Dunes in which they introduced grazing in the 80s and then slowly expanded. Some former control plots were suddenly grazed and then replaced by new control plots... But in principle they compare grazed vs ungrazed...
design_notes: a bit chaotic, had to take some decisions re sample size. Looks like overall 85 grazed surveys, 94 ungrazed surveys across years. 39 locations in total, 21 in dune slacks (54%), 18 in dry dune. Splitted the number of surveys accordingly, but not sure if thats true? Overall, interesting paper, not very meta-analysis friendly.
land_use_history_notes: In the past few centuries, activities such as marram grass cutting, low-intensity grazing with domestic livestock and the usage of the site as an extensive rabbit warren helped maintain the system in a physically mobile state, with landward movement of dunes and the creation of new dune slacks and blow-outs occurring (Rhind et al. 2001). Up until the 1940s much of the system remained highly mobile (Rhind et al. 2001). However, after the Second World War, the dunes were left rather unmanaged with little or no stocking (Hurford & Perry 2001). The afforestation of approximately half of the site with conifers between the 1940s and 1960s, the cessation of stock grazing, an increased deposition of atmospheric N, the decline of the marram weaving industry and decline of rabbit populations because of an outbreak of myxomatosis, which first reached Newborough Warren in 1954 (Rhind et al. 2001; Jones et al. 2008) may all have contributed to the increased stabilization of the dunes and succession towards more mature vegetation. As a consequence, the previously short swards changed to tall grass and tall herb communities, low-growing species and areas of bare sand were lost, and shrubs invaded the grasslands (Ranwell 1960; Hope-Jones 1964; Hodgkin 1984). Today, the dominant vegetation types are semi-fixed and fixed dune grasslands and mature slacks (Rhind et al. 2001).
plot_number: very confusing, 18 in dune habitats and 21 in dune slacks
introduced_herbivores: Bos primigenius taurus; Equus ferus caballus
herbivore_manipulation_notes: all over the place. Some in some enclosures, then new ones added etc
density_high_megafauna: NA Bos primigenius taurus; 0.28 Equus ferus caballus

land_use_history_notes: In the past few centuries, activities such as marram grass cutting, low-intensity grazing with domestic livestock and the usage of the site as an extensive rabbit warren helped maintain the system in a physically mobile state, with landward movement of dunes and the creation of new dune slacks and blow-outs occurring (Rhind et al. 2001). However, after the Second World War, the dunes were left rather unmanaged with little or no stocking (Hurford & Perry 2001). As a consequence, the previously short swards changed to tall grass and tall herb communities, low-growing species and areas of bare sand were lost, and shrubs invaded the grasslands (Ranwell 1960; Hope-Jones 1964; Hodgkin 1984). Today, the dominant vegetation types are semi-fixed and fixed dune grasslands and mature slacks (Rhind et al. 2001).
